# 1.1 Why marketing runs on data {.divider background-color="#0a3d6e"}

## The manager's job description has changed

::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
::: incremental
-   Every purchase, click, swipe, and like leaves a trace — firms sit on more behavioral data than they can use
-   Surveys of CMOs consistently rank **data & analytics competence** among the top changes to the marketing role
-   The bottleneck is no longer *collecting* data — it is **drawing valid conclusions** from it
:::
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

<!-- ::: source -->
<!-- Source: Deloitte CMO Insights (2024) -->
<!-- ::: -->
:::
:::

::: keybox
This course is **not** about producing numbers. It is about knowing **which analysis answers which managerial question** — and executing it credibly in R.

Keep to ≤ 5 minutes. One exhibit is enough; the eBay case carries the real motivation.

# 1.2 A \$50 million question {.divider background-color="#0a3d6e"}

## eBay, 2012: does paid search advertising pay off?

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
-   eBay spent \~ \$50M **per year** on paid search ads (Google, Bing, Yahoo)
-   The analytics team examined the data: users **exposed to ads bought far more** than users who weren't
-   Measured "returns" on brand-keyword ads looked spectacular
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r ebay-naive, fig.width=6, fig.height=4.6}
fig_ebay_naive()
```
:::
:::

::: discussion
**Discuss (5 min):** Would you keep spending the \$50M? What could go wrong with this conclusion?
:::

::: notes
Collect hypotheses on the board before revealing. Students usually find "people who search for eBay would have gone there anyway" — perfect setup.
:::

## What the experiment revealed

::: incremental
-   In 2012, economists convinced eBay to run a **large-scale experiment**: paid search was **switched off** in randomly selected US regions and kept on in others
-   Result: sales in the switched-off regions **barely moved** — most clicks came from people who **would have bought anyway**
-   The naive analysis had compared **shoppers with intent** to **shoppers without intent** — and credited the difference to the ads
-   Estimated true returns for the average keyword: **negative**
:::

. . .

::: keybox
Smart people, huge data, careful computation — and a conclusion that was off by tens of millions of dollars. **The problem was not the math. It was the comparison.**
:::

::: source
Case based on Blake, Nosko & Tadelis (2015), *Econometrica* — details in the course book.
:::

## The comparison that matters

**The causal question:** *What would eBay's sales have been **without** the ads — everything else unchanged?*

<br>

|                                | Observed              | Needed                             |
|--------------------------------|-----------------------|-------------------------------------|
| Group A                        | Exposed users' sales  | Exposed users' sales                |
| Group B                        | Unexposed users' sales| **The same users**, unexposed       |
| Difference measures…           | Exposure **+ intent** | Effect of exposure only             |

<br>

::: keybox
The "needed" Group B is a **counterfactual** — a world we can never observe directly. All of causal inference is about **constructing a credible stand-in** for it. This single idea organizes the entire course.
:::

# 1.3 Four kinds of questions {.divider background-color="#0a3d6e"}

## Every analytics task answers one of four questions {.smaller}

| # | Question | Type | Marketing examples |
|---|----------------------------|-------------|----------------------------------------|
| 1 | **What is going on?** | Descriptive | Segment sizes, churn rate, funnel drop-off, satisfaction tracking |
| 2 | **What will happen?** | Predictive | Which customers will churn next quarter? Demand next month? |
| 3 | **What happens if we act?** | Causal | Does the discount *cause* extra sales? Did the campaign work? |
| 4 | **What should we do?** | Prescriptive | Set the price; allocate budget across channels |

. . .

::: keybox
**Prescription requires causation.** To choose an action you must know what each action would *cause* — i.e., compare counterfactuals. Prediction alone is not enough… and confusing 2 with 3 is precisely the eBay mistake.
:::

::: notes
Anchor each row with a quick show of hands: "who has seen a dashboard like this?" The table returns as the orientation slide of every future session.
:::

## Prediction ≠ causation: same data, different questions

**"Customers who see our newsletter churn 40% less."**

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**As a predictive statement ✓**

Newsletter readership *predicts* retention — useful for **targeting**: flag non-readers as churn risks.

*Valid even if the newsletter does nothing.*
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**As a causal statement ✗ (so far)**

"Send more newsletters → churn drops"?\
Only if readership *causes* retention — but engaged customers **both** read newsletters **and** stay.

*Requires a counterfactual comparison.*
:::
:::

. . .

::: discussion
**Classify these (2 min, neighbor discussion):** (a) "Which ad creative will get the highest CTR?" (b) "How large is our Gen-Z segment?" (c) "Should we raise the price by 5%?"
:::

# 1.4 Correlation, causation & what data can show {.divider background-color="#0a3d6e"}

## Two pictures of "X relates to Y"

```{r two-pictures, fig.width=12.5, fig.height=5}
fig_two_pictures()
```

::: keybox
The two pictures can look **equally convincing** — yet only (a) licenses a causal conclusion. The difference is invisible in the plot: it lies in **how the data came to be** (the *data-generating process*).
:::

## Three ways to get the same scatter plot

```{r three-scatters, fig.width=12.5, fig.height=4.6}
fig_three_scatters()
```

::: incremental
-   All three panels show a similar positive correlation — **the data alone cannot distinguish them**
-   Panel 2: the relationship is created by a third variable (color = customer segment) — **within** each segment, it vanishes
-   Panel 3: any two trending series correlate — time is the ultimate confounder
:::

::: notes
These are simulated, so *we* know the truth in each panel — make that explicit: "I generated these; the labels are correct by construction. With real data, you never get the labels for free."
:::

## Reverse causality: who is causing whom?

**Observed:** regions with higher ad spend show higher sales.

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r reverse-1, fig.width=5.6, fig.height=2.2}
dgm_reverse("forward")
```

*Story 1:* advertising drives sales.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r reverse-2, fig.width=5.6, fig.height=2.2}
dgm_reverse("backward")
```

*Story 2:* budgets are **set as a % of sales** — sales drive ad spend.
:::
:::

::: keybox
Both stories produce identical data. Marketing budget rules make reverse causality a **routine** hazard in marketing data, not an exotic one.
:::

# 1.5 The cast of variables {.divider background-color="#0a3d6e"}

## The two lead roles

```{r dv-iv, fig.width=8, fig.height=2.4, fig.align='center'}
dgm_dv_iv()
```

-   **Outcome / dependent variable (DV):** the quantity the manager cares about
-   **Treatment / independent variable (IV):** the lever the manager can pull

::: keybox
Defining these two precisely — *whose* purchases, over *what horizon*, *which* discount — is half of research design (§1.8).
:::

## The villain: the confounder

::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r confounder, fig.width=6.2, fig.height=4}
dgm_confounder()
```
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
-   Causes **both** treatment and outcome
-   Creates correlation **without** causation — panel 2 of our gallery
-   **The eBay confounder:** purchase intent → people search for "eBay" → see the ad → and buy anyway
-   Whole toolkits (Ch. 5–6) exist to deal with confounders in observational data
:::
:::

## Supporting roles: mediator and moderator {.smaller}

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r mediator, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.4}
dgm_mediator()
```

**Mediator — the *how***

Lies **on the path**: the mechanism through which X works.\
Why care? It tells you **what to optimize** (creative that builds awareness).
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r moderator, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.4}
dgm_moderator()
```

**Moderator — the *for whom / when***

Points **at the arrow**: changes the **strength** of the effect.\
"The discount works for new customers, not loyal ones."
:::
:::

. . .

::: keybox
Today: **recognize** the roles. Chapter 5 teaches how to **handle** each one — and shows that mishandling them (e.g., "controlling" for a mediator) can wreck an analysis.
:::

## The full cast around one causal question

```{r full-cast, fig.width=10.5, fig.height=4.8, fig.align='center'}
dgm_full_cast()
```

::: notes
This figure is the recurring visual anchor — it reappears verbatim at the start of Ch. 5 (mediation/moderation) and Ch. 6. Blue = your question; red = threatens it; green = explains it; orange = qualifies it.
:::

# 1.6 Why randomization works {.divider background-color="#0a3d6e"}

## Randomization cuts every arrow into the treatment

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r random-dag, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.8}
dgm_randomization()
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: incremental
-   Assignment now depends **only on the coin** — not on intent, engagement, income, mood, …
-   Confounders (known **and unknown**) are balanced across groups *in expectation*
-   The control group becomes a valid **counterfactual**: same kinds of people, minus the treatment
-   Differences in outcomes can then be attributed to the treatment (up to chance — quantified in Ch. 3)
:::
:::
:::

## "Balanced — even on what we never measured"

```{r balance, fig.width=12, fig.height=4.6}
fig_balance()
```

::: keybox
Left: the groups differ systematically — including on **intent**, which we (realistically) never observe. Right: one coin flip balances everything at once, **without knowing what needs balancing**. That is the magic randomization buys.
:::

## The price of observational data

**Causal conclusions from observational data require assuming:**

::: keybox
**No unobserved confounders** — every variable that drives both treatment and outcome has been measured and correctly adjusted for.
:::

::: incremental
-   This assumption is **untestable in principle**: you cannot check balance on variables you did not observe
-   Experiments **buy** the assumption *by design*; observational studies must **argue** for it — with domain knowledge, not statistics
-   This asymmetry is the most important sentence of the course: it determines what your data can and cannot claim
-   It is *not* a counsel of despair — Ch. 5–6 develop the toolkit for making the argument as credible as possible
:::

::: notes
If one idea survives from today, it should be this slide. Refer back to it whenever a student says "we controlled for everything".
:::

# 1.7 Between the poles: quasi-experiments {.divider background-color="#0a3d6e"}

## Sometimes the world randomizes for you (almost)

**A spectrum of designs:**

| | Experiment | Quasi-experiment | Observational |
|---|---|---|---|
| Who assigns treatment? | The researcher (coin flip) | External event / rule | The units themselves |
| Example | A/B test of a discount | Platform launches in some countries first | Newsletter readers vs. non-readers |
| Key requirement | Correct execution | "As-good-as-random" timing/rule | **No unobserved confounders** |

. . .

-   Policy changes, staggered rollouts, regional boundaries → treatment variation **not chosen by the units**
-   Workhorse method: **difference-in-differences** — compare *changes* in treated vs. untreated markets
-   Extremely common in practice (and in marketing research) → dedicated session in **Module 6 (panel data)**

::: notes
Insert a one-slide teaser from your own research here — e.g., a streaming-platform entry staggered across markets. Concrete beats abstract for the preview.
:::

# 1.8 From business problem to research design {.divider background-color="#0a3d6e"}

## The translation template

**Manager:** *"I want to know whether our loyalty program is worth the money."*

| Design element | Your translation |
|---|---|
| **Outcome (DV)** | Customer contribution margin, 12 months |
| **Treatment (IV)** | Loyalty program membership |
| **Unit of analysis** | Customer |
| **Question type** | Causal (→ prescriptive decision) |
| **Likely confounders** | Purchase frequency & engagement *before* joining |
| **Feasible design?** | Randomize invitations? Staggered regional rollout? Observational + adjustment? |

::: keybox
A precise, falsifiable formulation ("membership increases 12-month margin") beats a vague aspiration ("the program creates value") — it dictates data, design, and analysis.
:::

## Your turn (pairs, 10 min)

::: discussion
**Translate one of these into the template:**

1.  "Should we invest more in influencer marketing?"
2.  "Is our app driving retention, or do loyal customers just download the app?"
3.  "Did last spring's rebranding damage sales in Germany?"

For each: DV, IV, unit, question type, two plausible confounders, and the **best feasible design** (experiment / quasi-experiment / observational).
:::

::: notes
Debrief: #2 is reverse causality on a silver platter; #3 has no possible experiment (one-shot event) → motivates quasi-experimental thinking with comparison markets.
:::

# 1.9 The analytics workflow — and AI assistants {.divider background-color="#0a3d6e"}

## Where AI helps — and where it cannot replace you {.smaller}

| Workflow step | Nature of the work | AI assistant… |
|---|---|---|
| Formulate the question | **Judgment** | can challenge you — cannot know your business |
| Choose design & method | **Judgment** | suggests options — *you* own the assumptions |
| Write & debug R code | Mechanical | **excellent** — use it freely, including in this course |
| Interpret results | **Judgment** | drafts text — but cannot verify the causal claim |
| Communicate to stakeholders | Mixed | strong support, needs your framing |

. . .

::: keybox
**Course policy in one line:** use AI to *accelerate* your learning of the judgment steps, not to *skip* them. Assessments in this course are designed so that the judgment steps are what earns the points.
:::

::: notes
Be explicit and non-moralizing. Demo (2 min): a lazy prompt ("analyze this data") vs. a good prompt (states DV, IV, design, asks for assumptions) — same tool, different learning.
:::

| Module | Sessions | Driving question |

::: keybox
**Group project preview:** design a survey **containing a real randomized experiment**, field it, analyze it. Everything from today — counterfactuals, randomization, confounders — becomes something you *build*, not just recognize.
:::

## Learning check — can you spot the reasoning? {.smaller}

1.  An analyst reports: *"App users have 2× the lifetime value of non-users — the app clearly pays off."* Which question type is being **answered**, which is being **claimed**? Name the most plausible confounder.
2.  A platform's advertising dashboard compares purchases of users who clicked an ad vs. users who saw it and didn't click. Is this an experiment? What role does "interest in the product" play?
3.  Your CMO wants to know whether to extend a price promotion nationally after a pilot in Vienna. What design element makes the pilot informative — and what is the counterfactual?
4.  For each: newsletter → *(opens →)* purchases; discount effect stronger for students — mediator or moderator?

::: notes
These four map onto: (1) prediction vs. causation + confounder, (2) selection bias in platform tools — bridge to Ch. 4, (3) counterfactual thinking, (4) mediator/moderator vocabulary.
:::
